questionText: A simply-supported rectangular reinforced concrete beam has a width 250 mm and an overall depth 600 mm. The effective span of the beam is 6.23 m. The beam carries a live load of 5 kN/m and super imposed dead load of 5 kN/m, in addition to its own weight. The unit weight of reinforced concrete is 25 $kN/m^3$ . Consider the load factor of 1.5 for all stated loads. The design bending moment (in kN·m) for the limit state of collapse is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Given: b = 250 mm, overall depth D = 600 mm, span L = 6.23 m
Live load = 5 kN/m, SIDL = 5 kN/m, Unit weight of RC = 25 kN/m3kN/m^3kN/m3, Load factor = 1.5

Step 1 - Self weight of beam:
wSW=b×D×γ=0.25×0.60×25=3.75 kN/mw_{SW} = b \times D \times \gamma = 0.25 \times 0.60 \times 25 = 3.75 \text{ kN/m}wSW​=b×D×γ=0.25×0.60×25=3.75 kN/m

Step 2 - Total factored load:
wu=1.5×(wLL+wSIDL+wSW)=1.5×(5+5+3.75)=1.5×13.75=20.625 kN/mw_u = 1.5 \times (w_{LL} + w_{SIDL} + w_{SW}) = 1.5 \times (5 + 5 + 3.75) = 1.5 \times 13.75 = 20.625 \text{ kN/m}wu​=1.5×(wLL​+wSIDL​+wSW​)=1.5×(5+5+3.75)=1.5×13.75=20.625 kN/m

Step 3 - Design bending moment (simply supported):
Mu=wuL28=20.625×(6.23)28=20.625×38.818=800.58=100.06 kN.mM_u = \dfrac{w_u L^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times (6.23)^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times 38.81}{8} = \dfrac{800.5}{8} = \mathbf{100.06 \text{ kN.m}}Mu​=8wu​L2​=820.625×(6.23)2​=820.625×38.81​=8800.5​=100.06 kN.m
explanationText: Given: b = 250 mm, overall depth D = 600 mm, span L = 6.23 mLive load = 5 kN/m, SIDL = 5 kN/m, Unit weight of RC = 25 $kN/m^3$ , Load factor = 1.5Step 1 - Self weight of beam: $w_{SW} = b \times D \times \gamma = 0.25 \times 0.60 \times 25 = 3.75 \text{ kN/m}$ Step 2 - Total factored load: $w_u = 1.5 \times (w_{LL} + w_{SIDL} + w_{SW}) = 1.5 \times (5 + 5 + 3.75) = 1.5 \times 13.75 = 20.625 \text{ kN/m}$ Step 3 - Design bending moment (simply supported): $M_u = \dfrac{w_u L^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times (6.23)^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times 38.81}{8} = \dfrac{800.5}{8} = \mathbf{100.06 \text{ kN.m}}$

questionText: A 250 mm wide x 600 mm deep rectangular concrete beam is prestressed by means of 4 high-tensile tendons, each of 14 mm diameter. P=4×At×fpe=4×153.86×700=430808 N≈430.8 kNP = 4 \times A_t \times f_{pe} = 4 \times 153.86 \times 700 = 430808 \text{ N} \approx 430.8 \text{ kN}P=4×At​×fpe​=4×153.86×700=430808 N≈430.8 kN

Centroid of beam from soffit = 600/2 = 300 mm
e=300−200=100 mme = 300 - 200 = 100 \text{ mm}e=300−200=100 mm

Step 4 - Section modulus (bottom fibre):
Zb=bD26=250×60026=250×3600006=15×106 mm3Z_b = \dfrac{bD^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 600^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 360000}{6} = 15 \times 10^6 \text{ mm}^3Zb​=6bD2​=6250×6002​=6250×360000​=15×106 mm3

Step 5 - Maximum BM without tension at soffit:
Stress at soffit = PA+PeZb−MZb≥0\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b} - \dfrac{M}{Z_b} \geq 0AP​+Zb​Pe​−Zb​M​≥0
M≤(PA+PeZb)×Zb=P⋅ZbA+P⋅eM \leq \left(\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b}\right) \times Z_b = P \cdot \dfrac{Z_b}{A} + P \cdot eM≤(AP​+Zb​Pe​)×Zb​=P⋅AZb​​+P⋅e
A=250×600=150000 mm2A = 250 \times 600 = 150000 \text{ mm}^2A=250×600=150000 mm2
M≤430.8×15×106150000+430.8×100M \leq 430.8 \times \dfrac{15 \times 10^6}{150000} + 430.8 \times 100M≤430.8×15000015×106​+430.8×100
M≤430.8×100+430.8×100=43080+43080=86160 kN mm=86.2 kN mM \leq 430.8 \times 100 + 430.8 \times 100 = 43080 + 43080 = 86160 \text{ kN mm} = 86.2 \text{ kN m}M≤430.8×100+430.8×100=43080+43080=86160 kN mm=86.2 kN m
explanationText: Given: Beam: 250 mm wide x 600 mm deep. 4 tendons of 14 mm diameter, centred 200 mm from soffit. Effective stress $= 700 N/mm^2. \; \pi = 3.14$ Step 1 - Area of each tendon: $A_t = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 14^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 196}{4} = \dfrac{615.44}{4} = 153.86 \text{ mm}^2$ Step 2 - Total prestress force P: $P = 4 \times A_t \times f_{pe} = 4 \times 153.86 \times 700 = 430808 \text{ N} \approx 430.8 \text{ kN}$ Step 3 - Eccentricity e (from centroid to tendon):Centroid of beam from soffit = 600/2 = 300 mm $e = 300 - 200 = 100 \text{ mm}$ Step 4 - Section modulus (bottom fibre): $Z_b = \dfrac{bD^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 600^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 360000}{6} = 15 \times 10^6 \text{ mm}^3$ Step 5 - Maximum BM without tension at soffit:Stress at soffit = $\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b} - \dfrac{M}{Z_b} \geq 0$ $M \leq \left(\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b}\right) \times Z_b = P \cdot \dfrac{Z_b}{A} + P \cdot e$ $A = 250 \times 600 = 150000 \text{ mm}^2$ $M \leq 430.8 \times \dfrac{15 \times 10^6}{150000} + 430.8 \times 100$ $M \leq 430.8 \times 100 + 430.8 \times 100 = 43080 + 43080 = 86160 \text{ kN mm} = 86.2 \text{ kN m}$

A rectangular singly reinforced concrete beam has a width of 300 mm and an effective depth of 550 mm. The grades of steel and concrete are Fe500 and M25, respectively. The area of steel in tension is 1963 mm2mm^2mm2. The depth of neutral axis is 302 mm. The most probable mode of failure of the beam is:
questionText: A rectangular singly reinforced concrete beam has a width of 300 mm and an effective depth of 550 mm. The grades of steel and concrete are Fe500 and M25, respectively. The area of steel in tension is 1963 $mm^2$ . The depth of neutral axis is 302 mm. The ratio of the limiting depth of the neutral axis $(x_{u,max})$ to the effective depth $(d)$ of the beam is 0.456.The most probable mode of failure of the beam is:
explanationHtml:
Actual neutral axis depth xu=302x_u = 302xu​=302 mm
Effective depth d=550d = 550d=550 mm
xu,max/d=0.456x_{u,max}/d = 0.456xu,max​/d=0.456 → \rightarrow → xu,max=0.456×550=250.8x_{u,max} = 0.456 \times 550 = 250.8xu,max​=0.456×550=250.8 mm

Comparison:
xu=302 mm>xu,max=250.8 mmx_u = 302 \text{ mm} > x_{u,max} = 250.8 \text{ mm}xu​=302 mm>xu,max​=250.8 mm

Interpretation:
When actual neutral axis depth exceeds the limiting value, the beam is over-reinforced.

In an over-reinforced beam:
Concrete reaches its limiting strain (0.0035) before steel yields
Failure occurs by crushing of concrete in compression
This is a sudden, brittle failure mode

Therefore, The most probable mode of failure is compression failure.
explanationText: Actual neutral axis depth $x_u = 302$ mmEffective depth $d = 550$ mm $x_{u,max}/d = 0.456$ $\rightarrow$ $x_{u,max} = 0.456 \times 550 = 250.8$ mmComparison: $x_u = 302 \text{ mm} > x_{u,max} = 250.8 \text{ mm}$ Interpretation:When actual neutral axis depth exceeds the limiting value, the beam is over-reinforced.In an over-reinforced beam: Concrete reaches its limiting strain (0.0035) before steel yields Failure occurs by crushing of concrete in compression This is a sudden, brittle failure modeTherefore, The most probable mode of failure is compression failure.

questionMarkup: Select ALL CORRECT option(s) which can be considered to check whether the flexural stresses in a prestressed concrete beam are within the allowable stresses at the transfer and the service stages.
questionText: Select ALL CORRECT option(s) which can be considered to check whether the flexural stresses in a prestressed concrete beam are within the allowable stresses at the transfer and the service stages.
explanationHtml:
Methods to check flexural stresses in prestressed concrete beams:

(A) Limiting zone (cable zone / pressure line zone):
Defines the zone within which the prestressing force must lie to keep stresses within allowable limits at both transfer and service stages.

(B) Magnel's diagram:
A graphical method that plots the relationship between 1/P1/P1/P and eee (eccentricity) from the four stress conditions (two at transfer, two at service). The feasible zone gives all valid combinations.

(C) Hoyer effect:
Refers to the lateral expansion of pre-tensioned tendons upon release, creating bond. Not used for stress checks.

(D) Load balancing method:
Used for deflection and design of prestress, not specifically for checking allowable stress compliance.
explanationText: Methods to check flexural stresses in prestressed concrete beams:(A) Limiting zone (cable zone / pressure line zone):Defines the zone within which the prestressing force must lie to keep stresses within allowable limits at both transfer and service stages. (B) Magnel's diagram:A graphical method that plots the relationship between $1/P$ and $e$ (eccentricity) from the four stress conditions (two at transfer, two at service). The feasible zone gives all valid combinations. (C) Hoyer effect:Refers to the lateral expansion of pre-tensioned tendons upon release, creating bond. Not used for stress checks. (D) Load balancing method:Used for deflection and design of prestress, not specifically for checking allowable stress compliance.

subject: RCC Structures
topic: Concrete Technology
questionMarkup: Which one of the following is utilized to determine the long-term deformation of concrete under sustained loading?
questionText: Which one of the following is utilized to determine the long-term deformation of concrete under sustained loading?
explanationHtml:
Definitions:

Creep: Time-dependent deformation of concrete under sustained (long-term) loading at constant stress. It is the phenomenon used to determine long-term deformation.

Shrinkage: Volume change due to loss of moisture - not load-dependent.

Modulus of Rupture: Flexural tensile strength of concrete - measured by beam bending test.

Split Tensile Strength: Indirect tensile strength - measured by splitting a cylinder.

Therefore, Creep is the property used to determine long-term deformation under sustained loading.
explanationText: Definitions: Creep: Time-dependent deformation of concrete under sustained (long-term) loading at constant stress. It is the phenomenon used to determine long-term deformation. Shrinkage: Volume change due to loss of moisture - not load-dependent. Modulus of Rupture: Flexural tensile strength of concrete - measured by beam bending test. Split Tensile Strength: Indirect tensile strength - measured by splitting a cylinder.Therefore, Creep is the property used to determine long-term deformation under sustained loading.

questionText: The design shear strength of a reinforced concrete rectangular beam with a width of $250\text{mm}$ and an effective depth of $500\text{mm}$ , is $0.3\text{MPa}$ . The torsional moment capacity of the section (in kN.m) under pure torsion, as per IS 456:2000, is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
explanationHtml:
Given:
b=250mmb = 250\text{mm}b=250mm
d=500mmd = 500\text{mm}d=500mm

Using empirical torsional stress:
τeq=0.162N/mm2\tau_{eq} = 0.162\text{N/mm}^2τeq​=0.162N/mm2
Apply torsional moment formula (with 1.7 partial factor):
Tc=τeq⋅(11.7)⋅b⋅d2T_c = \tau_{eq} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1.7}\right) \cdot b \cdot d^2Tc​=τeq​⋅(1.71​)⋅b⋅d2

Substitute values:
Tc=0.162⋅0.588⋅250⋅250000=5.955kN.mT_c = 0.162 \cdot 0.588 \cdot 250 \cdot 250000 = 5.955 \text{kN.m}Tc​=0.162⋅0.588⋅250⋅250000=5.955kN.m

Answer: 6.0kN.m\boxed{6.0 \text{kN.m}}6.0kN.m​
explanationText: Given: $b = 250\text{mm}$ $d = 500\text{mm}$ Using empirical torsional stress: $\tau_{eq} = 0.162\text{N/mm}^2$ Apply torsional moment formula (with 1.7 partial factor): $T_c = \tau_{eq} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1.7}\right) \cdot b \cdot d^2$ Substitute values: $T_c = 0.162 \cdot 0.588 \cdot 250 \cdot 250000 = 5.955 \text{kN.m}$ Answer: $\boxed{6.0 \text{kN.m}}$

questionText: If the weights retained on the $2.36 \mathrm{~mm}, 1.18 \mathrm{~mm}, 600 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ , and $300 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ sieves are $30 \%$ , $35 \%, 15 \%$ , and $20 \%$ , respectively, of the total weight of an aggregate sample, then the fineness modulus of the sample is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
explanationHtml:
To calculate the Fineness Modulus (FM), we take the cumulative percentage retained on each standard sieve and divide the sum by 100.

Given weights retained:
On 2.36 mm sieve = 30%
On 1.18 mm sieve = 35%
On 600 μm\mu mμm sieve = 15%
On 300 μm\mu mμm sieve = 20%

Step 1: Compute cumulative percentages retained:
- 2.36 mm sieve: 30% 30\% 30%
- 1.18 mm sieve: 30+35=65% 30 + 35 = 65\% 30+35=65%
- 600 μm\mu mμm sieve: 65+15=80% 65 + 15 = 80\% 65+15=80%
- 300 μm\mu mμm sieve: 80+20=100% 80 + 20 = 100\% 80+20=100%

Step 2: Sum of cumulative percentages retained:
30+65+80+100=275 30 + 65 + 80 + 100 = 275 30+65+80+100=275

Step 3: Fineness Modulus:
FM=275100=2.75 \text{FM} = \frac{275}{100} = 2.75 FM=100275​=2.75

Final Answer: 2.75 \boxed{2.75} 2.75​

questionText: As per IS 456:2000 provisions for two-way slabs with continuous edges, the longitudinal steel reinforcement to be provided in the edge strip is based on

options.html: the area of longitudinal steel provided in the middle strip in the shorter span
options.text: the area of longitudinal steel provided in the middle strip in the shorter span

options.html: the area of longitudinal steel provided in the middle strip in the longer span
options.text: the area of longitudinal steel provided in the middle strip in the longer span

options.html: the prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs
options.text: the prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

explanationHtml:
As per IS 456:2000, in the design of two-way slabs with continuous edges, the slab is divided into middle strips and edge strips. The bending moment is primarily resisted by the middle strip, while the edge strip is provided mainly for distribution and minimum reinforcement.

According to Clause 27.4.3 of IS 456:2000:
Reinforcement in the edge strip is not based on calculated moments or reinforcement in the middle strip. Instead, it is based on the prescribed minimum requirement for slabs.

Therefore,
Reinforcement in edge strip = Prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

Final Answer:
The prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

options.html: Area of tension reinforcement is decreased.

options.html: Area of compression reinforcement is decreased.
options.text: Area of compression reinforcement is decreased.

explanationHtml:
In a doubly reinforced balance section, the Ast A_{st} Ast​ and Asc A_{sc} Asc​ are such that the depth of neutral axis is xu,limx_{u,lim}xu,lim​ or xbalx_{bal}xbal​.
To make the above section an under-reinforced section, the strength of compression side has to be increased compared to that of tension side.
This can be done by either increasing the amount of compression reinforcement or decreasing the amount of tension reinforcement.
Hence, the correct options are (B) and (C)

explanationHtml:
While removing the props, we need to ensure that the beam type does not change i.e. if it is a cantilever beam then the props shall be removed in such a manner that the beam at the intermediate stage also shows cantilever behaviour.
If we remove prop 'S1' first then tensile stress will be generated at the bottom and no structural reinforcement is there to take care of this tension.
So, correct order is S5 → \rightarrow →S4 → \rightarrow → S3 → \rightarrow → S2 → \rightarrow → S1

questionText: With regard to the shear design of RCC beams, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.html: Excessive shear reinforcement can lead to compression failure in concrete
options.text: Excessive shear reinforcement can lead to compression failure in concrete

options.html: Beams without shear reinforcement, even if adequately designed for flexure, can have brittle failure
options.text: Beams without shear reinforcement, even if adequately designed for flexure, can have brittle failure

options.html: The main (longitudinal) reinforcement plays no role in the shear resistance of beam
options.text: The main (longitudinal) reinforcement plays no role in the shear resistance of beam

options.html: As per IS456:2000, the nominal shear stress in the beams of varying depth depends on both the design shear force as well as the design bending moment
options.text: As per IS456:2000, the nominal shear stress in the beams of varying depth depends on both the design shear force as well as the design bending moment

explanationHtml:
Option A is true, because when the area of shear reinforcement is large i.e. in case of excessive shear reinforcement, concrete becomes stronger is diagonal tension on failure compared to diagonal compression failure and compression failure may occur before the shear reinforcement has yielded.
Option 'BBB' is true because for beams without shear reinforcement, once the flexural crack crosses the longitudinal reinforcement, the propagation of crack will be sudden and there can be brittle failure.
Option 'CCC' is not true, as main reinforcement increases the shear resitance by providing dowel action, limiting crack width and by increasing the depth of concrete. Design shear strength of concrete is a function of grade of concree and percentage tensile reinforcement.
Option 'D' is true, as for beams with varying depth, nominal shear stress,
τv=Vu±Mutan⁡βdbd(\tau_{v}=\frac{V_{u} \pm \frac{M_{u} \tan \beta}{d}}{b d}(τv​=bdVu​±dMu​tanβ​​( clause 40.1.1, IS456: 2000)
it is dependent on both the design shear force and design bending moment.
Hence, options (A), (B) and (D) are true.
explanationText: Option A is true, because when the area of shear reinforcement is large i.e. in case of excessive shear reinforcement, concrete becomes stronger is diagonal tension on failure compared to diagonal compression failure and compression failure may occur before the shear reinforcement has yielded. Option ' $B$ ' is true because for beams without shear reinforcement, once the flexural crack crosses the longitudinal reinforcement, the propagation of crack will be sudden and there can be brittle failure. Option ' $C$ ' is not true, as main reinforcement increases the shear resitance by providing dowel action, limiting crack width and by increasing the depth of concrete. Design shear strength of concrete is a function of grade of concree and percentage tensile reinforcement. Option 'D' is true, as for beams with varying depth, nominal shear stress, $\tau_{v}=\frac{V_{u} \pm \frac{M_{u} \tan \beta}{d}}{b d}($ clause 40.1.1, IS456: 2000) it is dependent on both the design shear force and design bending moment. Hence, options (A), (B) and (D) are true.

explanationHtml:
This is a question of calculation of elastic shortening loss in post tensioned member.
Given data,
length = 15 m
b x D = 450 mm x 450 mm
Numberof tendons = 3
Cross-section area of each tendon (As)=200mm2 (A_s)=200 mm^2(As​)=200mm2.
Prestress = 1500 MPa
Modular ratio (m) = 6

From the given data, eccentricity (e) = 450/2-125 = 100 mm
Force in each cable (P)=1500×200×10−3=300kN(P) = 1500 \times 200 \times 10^{-3} = 300 kN(P)=1500×200×10−3=300kN
The tendons are tensioned one after another, and hence when tendon (1) is pulled no loss in tenson (1)
When tendon (2) is pulled, loss in tendon (1) but no loss in tendon (2).
When tendon (3) is pulled, loss in tendon (1) and (2), but no loss in tendon (3).
Hence, there will be 2 times losses in tendon (1), time loss in tendon (1) and no loss in tendon (3).
While calculating elastic shortening loss, self weight of the structure is neglected to be on the conservative side.
Consider tensioning of tendon-1

questionMarkup:
Read the following statements relating to flexure of reinforced concrete beams:

I. In over-reinforced sections, the failure strain in concrete reaches earlier than the yield strain in steel.
II. In under-reinforced sections, steel reaches yielding at a load lower than the load at which the concrete reaches failure strain.
III. Over-reinforced beams are recommended in practice as compared to the under-reinforced beams.
IV. In balanced sections, the concrete reaches failure strain earlier than the yield strain in tensile steel.

Each of the above statements is either True or False.
Which one of the following combinations is correct?
questionText: Read the following statements relating to flexure of reinforced concrete beams: I. In over-reinforced sections, the failure strain in concrete reaches earlier than the yield strain in steel. II. In under-reinforced sections, steel reaches yielding at a load lower than the load at which the concrete reaches failure strain. III. Over-reinforced beams are recommended in practice as compared to the under-reinforced beams. IV. In balanced sections, the concrete reaches failure strain earlier than the yield strain in tensile steel. Each of the above statements is either True or False. Which one of the following combinations is correct?
explanationHtml:
The question is based on LSM design principle as it is describing different conditions related to strain
Depending on amount of reinforcement in a cross- section, here ca be three types of sections viz. balanced, under reinforced and over reinforced.
Balanced section is a section that is expected to result in a balanced failure. It means at the ultimate limit state in flexure, the concrete will attain a limiting compressive strain of 0.0035 and steel will attain minimum specified tensile strain of 0.002+0.87fyEs0.002+\frac{0.87f_y}{E_s}0.002+Es​0.87fy​​
Under reinforced section is a section in which steel yield before collapse. Over reinforced section is a section in which crushing of concrete in compression i.e. attainment of compressive strain of 0.0035 occurs prior to yielding of steel.
In case of over reinforced section the deflection, crack width remain relatively low and failure occurs without any sign of warning and hence over reinforced flexural members are not recommended by IS code.
Based on the above information:
Statement I is true.
Statement II is true.
Statement III is false.
Statement IV is false.

Balancing load=Point load2Psin⁡θ=Q2P(eL/2)=22Pe×2L=W4PeL=We=WL4P=12000N×8000mm4×600×1000N=40mm\begin{aligned} \text{Balancing load} &= \text{Point load}\\ 2P \sin \theta &=Q\\ 2P\left ( \frac{e}{L/2} \right )&=2\\ \frac{2Pe \times 2}{L}&=W\\ \frac{4Pe}{L}&=W\\ e&=\frac{WL}{4P}\\ &=\frac{12000 N \times 8000mm}{4 \times 600 \times 1000N}\\ &=40mm \end{aligned}Balancing load2Psinθ2P(L/2e​)L2Pe×2​L4Pe​e​=Point load=Q=2=W=W=4PWL​=4×600×1000N12000N×8000mm​=40mm​
explanationText: P = 600 kN Simply supported span = L = 8 m To support a point load applied at mid span (W) = 12 kN $\begin{aligned} \text{Balancing load} &= \text{Point load}\\ 2P \sin \theta &=Q\\ 2P\left ( \frac{e}{L/2} \right )&=2\\ \frac{2Pe \times 2}{L}&=W\\ \frac{4Pe}{L}&=W\\ e&=\frac{WL}{4P}\\ &=\frac{12000 N \times 8000mm}{4 \times 600 \times 1000N}\\ &=40mm \end{aligned}$

questionText: When aspecimen of M25 concrete is loaded to a stress level of 12.5 MPa, a strain of $500 \times 10^{-6}$ is recorded. If this load is allowed to stand for a long time, the strain increasesto $1000 \times 10^{-6}$ . In accordance with the provisions of IS:456-2000, considering the long-term effects, the effective modulus of elasticity of the concrete (in MPa) is________
explanationHtml:
Effective modulus of elastic
Ece=Ec1+θEc=5000fck=500025=25000MPa\begin{aligned} E_{ce}&=\frac{E_c}{1+\theta } \\ E_c&= 5000\sqrt{f_{ck}}\\ &= 5000\sqrt{25}\\ &=25000MPa \end{aligned}Ece​Ec​​=1+θEc​​=5000fck​​=500025​=25000MPa​
Creep coefcient
θ=creep strainelastic strain=longterm strain - elastic strainelastic strain=(1000×10−6)−(500×10−6)(500×10−6)=1∴    Ece=250001+1=12500MPa\begin{aligned} \theta &=\frac{\text{creep strain}}{\text{elastic strain}} \\ &= \frac{\text{longterm strain - elastic strain}}{\text{elastic strain}}\\ &=\frac{(1000 \times 10^{-6})-(500 \times 10^{-6})}{(500 \times 10^{-6})}=1\\ \therefore \;\;E_{ce}&=\frac{25000}{1+1}=12500MPa \end{aligned}θ∴Ece​​=elastic straincreep strain​=elastic strainlongterm strain - elastic strain​=(500×10−6)(1000×10−6)−(500×10−6)​=1=1+125000​=12500MPa​
explanationText: Effective modulus of elastic $\begin{aligned} E_{ce}&=\frac{E_c}{1+\theta } \\ E_c&= 5000\sqrt{f_{ck}}\\ &= 5000\sqrt{25}\\ &=25000MPa \end{aligned}$ Creep coefcient $\begin{aligned} \theta &=\frac{\text{creep strain}}{\text{elastic strain}} \\ &= \frac{\text{longterm strain - elastic strain}}{\text{elastic strain}}\\ &=\frac{(1000 \times 10^{-6})-(500 \times 10^{-6})}{(500 \times 10^{-6})}=1\\ \therefore \;\;E_{ce}&=\frac{25000}{1+1}=12500MPa \end{aligned}$
explanationTex: \begin{aligned} \theta &=\frac{\text{creep strain}}{\text{elastic strain}} \\ &= \frac{\text{longterm strain - elastic strain}}{\text{elastic strain}}\\ &=\frac{(1000 \times 10^{-6})-(500 \times 10^{-6})}{(500 \times 10^{-6})}=1\\ \therefore \;\;E_{ce}&=\frac{25000}{1+1}=12500MPa \end{aligned}

Assuming that the reaction arrangement has rough interface and has the same properties that of soil, the factor of safety (round off to 1 decimal place) against shear failure is _____
explanationHtml:
Weight of Precast PCC block,
W=volume×γc=37.5×7.5×24=6750kNW=volume \times \gamma _c=37.5 \times 7.5 \times 24=6750kNW=volume×γc​=37.5×7.5×24=6750kN
Shear resistance below the Precast PCC block is,
S=C.A+Wtan⁡ϕS = C.A + W\tan \phiS=C.A+Wtanϕ
F.O safety against shear failure,
F=STF=C.A.+Wtan⁡ϕT=C.A.+Ntan⁡ϕT      (Since,  N=W)=17×37.5+6750×tan⁡25∘1875=2.0187≈2.0\begin{aligned} F&=\frac{S}{T} \\ F&=\frac{C.A.+W \tan \phi }{T} \\ &= \frac{C.A.+N \tan \phi }{T}\;\;\; (Since, \; N=W)\\ &= \frac{17 \times 37.5+6750 \times \tan 25^{\circ}}{1875}\\ &= 2.0187\approx 2.0 \end{aligned}FF​=TS​=TC.A.+Wtanϕ​=TC.A.+Ntanϕ​(Since,N=W)=187517×37.5+6750×tan25∘​=2.0187≈2.0​
explanationText: Weight of Precast PCC block, $W=volume \times \gamma _c=37.5 \times 7.5 \times 24=6750kN$ Shear resistance below the Precast PCC block is, $S = C.A + W\tan \phi$ F.O safety against shear failure, $\begin{aligned} F&=\frac{S}{T} \\ F&=\frac{C.A.+W \tan \phi }{T} \\ &= \frac{C.A.+N \tan \phi }{T}\;\;\; (Since, \; N=W)\\ &= \frac{17 \times 37.5+6750 \times \tan 25^{\circ}}{1875}\\ &= 2.0187\approx 2.0 \end{aligned}$

questionText: The frequency distribution of the compressive strength of 20 concrete cube specimens is given in the table. If $\mu$ is the mean strength of the specimens and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation, the number of specimens (out of 20) with compressive strength less than $\mu -3\sigma$ is ______
explanationHtml:
Average strength,
μ=(4×23)+(2×28)+(5×22.5)+(5×31)+(4×29)20=26.575MPaσ=Σ(μ−f)2n−1=(26.575−23)2×4+(26.575−28)2×2+(26.575−22.5)2×5+(26.575−31)2×5+(26.575−29)2×4(20−1)=3.7 \begin{aligned} \mu &=\frac{(4 \times 23)+(2 \times 28)+(5 \times 22.5)+(5 \times 31)+(4 \times 29)}{20} \\ &=26.575 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma &=\sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(\mu-f)^{2}}{n-1}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{\begin{array}{c} (26.575-23)^{2} \times 4+(26.575-28)^{2} \times 2\\ +(26.575-22.5)^{2} \times 5+(26.575-31)^{2} \\ \times 5+(26.575-29)^{2} \times 4 \end{array}}{(20-1)}} \\&=3.7 \end{aligned}μσ​=20(4×23)+(2×28)+(5×22.5)+(5×31)+(4×29)​=26.575MPa=n−1Σ(μ−f)2​​=(20−1)(26.575−23)2×4+(26.575−28)2×2+(26.575−22.5)2×5+(26.575−31)2×5+(26.575−29)2×4​​​=3.7​
Now, μ−3σ=26.575−3×3.7=15.48\mu-3 \sigma=26.575-3 \times 3.7=15.48 μ−3σ=26.575−3×3.7=15.48

explanationText: Average strength, $\begin{aligned} \mu &=\frac{(4 \times 23)+(2 \times 28)+(5 \times 22.5)+(5 \times 31)+(4 \times 29)}{20} \\ &=26.575 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma &=\sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(\mu-f)^{2}}{n-1}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{\begin{array}{c} (26.575-23)^{2} \times 4+(26.575-28)^{2} \times 2\\ +(26.575-22.5)^{2} \times 5+(26.575-31)^{2} \\ \times 5+(26.575-29)^{2} \times 4 \end{array}}{(20-1)}} \\&=3.7 \end{aligned}$ Now, $\mu-3 \sigma=26.575-3 \times 3.7=15.48$ Thus, no specimen is having compressive strength less than $\mu-3 \sigma.$

questionText: A pre-tensioned rectangular concrete beam 150 mm wide and 300 mm depth is prestressed with three straight tendons, each having a cross-sectional area of 50 $mm^{2}$ , to an initial stress of 1200 $N / mm^{2}$ . The tendons are located at 100 mm from the soffit of the beam. If the modular ratio is 6, the loss of prestressing force (in kN, up to one decimal place) due to the elastic deformation of concrete only is ______
explanationHtml:
Prestressing force,
P=3×50×1200=180000Ne=(D2−100)=(3002−100)=50mm \begin{aligned} P&=3 \times 50 \times 1200=180000 \mathrm{N} \\ e&=\left(\frac{D}{2}-100\right)=\left(\frac{300}{2}-100\right)=50 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}Pe​=3×50×1200=180000N=(2D​−100)=(2300​−100)=50mm​
Stress in concrete at the location of steel
=PA+P⋅eIe=180000150×300+180000×502(150×300312)=4.0+1.33=5.333 \begin{aligned} &=\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P \cdot e}{I} e\\ &=\frac{180000}{150 \times 300}+\frac{180000 \times 50^{2}}{\left(\frac{150 \times 300^{3}}{12}\right)} \\ &=4.0+1.33=5.333 \end{aligned}​=AP​+IP⋅e​e=150×300180000​+(12150×3003​)180000×502​=4.0+1.33=5.333​
Loss of stress
=m×fc=6×5.3333=32N/mm2 =m \times f_{c}=6 \times 5.3333=32 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}=m×fc​=6×5.3333=32N/mm2
Loss of prestressing force
=3×50×321000kN=4.8kN =\frac{3 \times 50 \times 32}{1000} \mathrm{kN}=4.8 \mathrm{kN}=10003×50×32​kN=4.8kN
explanationText: Prestressing force, $\begin{aligned} P&=3 \times 50 \times 1200=180000 \mathrm{N} \\ e&=\left(\frac{D}{2}-100\right)=\left(\frac{300}{2}-100\right)=50 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}$ Stress in concrete at the location of steel $\begin{aligned} &=\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P \cdot e}{I} e\\ &=\frac{180000}{150 \times 300}+\frac{180000 \times 50^{2}}{\left(\frac{150 \times 300^{3}}{12}\right)} \\ &=4.0+1.33=5.333 \end{aligned}$ Loss of stress $=m \times f_{c}=6 \times 5.3333=32 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ Loss of prestressing force $=\frac{3 \times 50 \times 32}{1000} \mathrm{kN}=4.8 \mathrm{kN}$

questionMarkup: According to the concept of Limit State Design as per IS 456: 2000, the probability of failure of a structure is__________.
questionText: According to the concept of Limit State Design as per IS 456: 2000, the probability of failure of a structure is__________.
explanationHtml:
The structure may fail when, the load exceeds the design load
(ii) the strength is less than the characteristic strength
(iii) both the load exceeds the design load and strength is less than the characteristic strength.
The probability of load exceeding design load = 5%
(iv) The probability of strength less than characteristic strength = 5%
The probability of failure is
=0.05×0.95+0.05×0.95+0.05×0.05 =0.05 \times 0.95+0.05 \times 0.95+0.05 \times 0.05 =0.05×0.95+0.05×0.95+0.05×0.05
=0.0975 =0.0975=0.0975
explanationText: The structure may fail when, the load exceeds the design load (ii) the strength is less than the characteristic strength (iii) both the load exceeds the design load and strength is less than the characteristic strength. The probability of load exceeding design load = 5% (iv) The probability of strength less than characteristic strength = 5% The probability of failure is $=0.05 \times 0.95+0.05 \times 0.95+0.05 \times 0.05$ $=0.0975$

Total stress in steel,
fs=PAs=150×103187.5=800MPa f_{s}=\frac{P}{A_{s}}=\frac{150 \times 10^{3}}{187.5}=800 \mathrm{MPa}fs​=As​P​=187.5150×103​=800MPa

=Δfsfs×100=49800×100=6.125% =\frac{\Delta f_{s}}{f_{s}} \times 100=\frac{49}{800} \times 100=6.125 \%=fs​Δfs​​×100=80049​×100=6.125%
explanationText: Stress in concrete at the level of tendon, $\begin{aligned} f_{c} &=\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P e^{2}}{I} \\ &=\frac{150 \times 10^{3}}{120 \times 200}+\frac{150 \times 20^{2} \times 12 \times 10^{3}}{120 \times 200^{3}} \\ &=7 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}$ Loss of prestress due to elastic deformation, $\Delta f_{s}=\frac{E_{s}}{E_{c}} \times f_{c}=\frac{2.1 \times 10^{5}}{3.0 \times 10^{4}} \times 7=49 \mathrm{MPa}$ Total stress in steel, $f_{s}=\frac{P}{A_{s}}=\frac{150 \times 10^{3}}{187.5}=800 \mathrm{MPa}$ $\therefore$ Percentage loss of stress $=\frac{\Delta f_{s}}{f_{s}} \times 100=\frac{49}{800} \times 100=6.125 \%$

questionText: Consider the following two statements related to reinforced concrete design, and identify whether they are TRUE of FALSE: I. Curtailment of bars in the flexural tension zone in beams reduces the shear strength at the cut-off locations. II. When a rectangular column section is subject to biaxially eccentric compression, the neutral axis will be parallel to the resultant axis of bending.

options.html: Both statements I and II are TRUE
options.text: Both statements I and II are TRUE

options.html: Statement I is TRUE, and statement II is FALSE
options.text: Statement I is TRUE, and statement II is FALSE

options.html: Statement I is FALSE, and statement II is TRUE
options.text: Statement I is FALSE, and statement II is TRUE

options.html: Both Statements I and II are FALSE
options.text: Both Statements I and II are FALSE

explanationHtml:
Statement I: Curtailment of bars in the flexural tension zone in beams reduces the shear strength at the cut-off locations.
This statement is TRUE because cutting tensile reinforcement decreases dowel action and reduces shear resistance at that location.

Statement II: When a rectangular column is subjected to biaxially eccentric compression, the neutral axis will be parallel to the resultant axis of bending.
This statement is FALSE because for biaxial bending, the neutral axis is governed by the interaction:
Mxy+Myx=0 M_x y + M_y x = 0 Mx​y+My​x=0
The slope of the neutral axis is:
slope of N.A.=−MyMx\text{slope of N.A.} = -\frac{M_y}{M_x} slope of N.A.=−Mx​My​​
Whereas the resultant bending axis has slope:
slope of resultant moment axis=MyMx\text{slope of resultant moment axis} =\frac{M_y}{M_x} slope of resultant moment axis=Mx​My​​
Thus, they are not parallel.
explanationText: Statement I: Curtailment of bars in the flexural tension zone in beams reduces the shear strength at the cut-off locations. This statement is TRUE because cutting tensile reinforcement decreases dowel action and reduces shear resistance at that location. Statement II: When a rectangular column is subjected to biaxially eccentric compression, the neutral axis will be parallel to the resultant axis of bending. This statement is FALSE because for biaxial bending, the neutral axis is governed by the interaction: $M_x y + M_y x = 0$ The slope of the neutral axis is: $\text{slope of N.A.} = -\frac{M_y}{M_x}$ Whereas the resultant bending axis has slope: $\text{slope of resultant moment axis} =\frac{M_y}{M_x}$ Thus, they are not parallel.
